concepts.title: The Barter System
concepts.definition: Before money, people bartered, exchanging goods directly: grain for cloth, cattle for salt; exchange worked only when each trader wanted exactly what the other offered, the double coincidence of wants.
concepts.key_idea: Barter ties every trade to luck: without a matching want on both sides, no deal can close.

concepts.title: Money as Medium of Exchange
concepts.definition: Money steps in as a medium everyone accepts: sell your goods for money, buy what you need with it; it also serves as a common measure of value, a store of savings and a standard for future payments.
concepts.key_idea: Money untangles trade: the farmer need not find a cloth-maker who wants grain, only a buyer who has money.

concepts.title: From Coins to Currency
concepts.definition: Metal coins stamped with kings' seals served trade for centuries, and paper currency backed by the state followed; India's rupee carries both a long history and the promise of the central bank.
concepts.key_idea: Money evolves with trade: from weighed metal to minted coin to printed note to digital transfer.

concepts.title: Exchange in a Market Economy
concepts.definition: With money, exchange grew into the market economy around us: prices express values, wages pay for work, and saving channels money to those who invest, linking present effort with future reward.
concepts.key_idea: Money made exchange so smooth that specialisation bloomed: do one thing well and trade for the rest.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does barter fail when the economy grows?

solution_template.explain: Each barter needs both sides to want the other's exact good at the same time.
With hundreds of goods, hunting a matching want costs more than the trade itself, so money's common acceptance wins.
